summary.text: An 84-year-old man tripped and fell at home the previous night after three glasses of whiskey and lay prone on the floor for about 12 hours, unable to move because of reduced upper limb mobility from a previous injury. He denied neck, back, hip or leg pain, and the crew found sensory and motor function intact on initial assessment.

After he was rolled upright, a scalp laceration and torticollis were noticed. In the ambulance there was torso bruising, urinary incontinence and a step-like deformity around C5 to C6, with intact distal sensory and motor function and initial observations recorded. Cervical collar immobilisation was not possible because of the torticollis, and a dressing was applied to the laceration.

While still in the ambulance his blood pressure unexpectedly dropped from 154/119 mmHg to 49/28 mmHg and he became less responsive. He was laid flat with legs raised (modified Trendelenburg position), given 500 ml sodium chloride and 100% oxygen, and responded well. A post-event ECG showed atrial bigeminy; the authors proposed several possible causes without establishing one.

He was transported under emergency conditions after pre-alerting the emergency department; on arrival blood pressure was 141/85 mmHg and Glasgow Coma Scale 15. At follow-up the next day he was on the orthopaedic ward with dislocated C3, C6 and C7 vertebrae, awaiting MRI, and ward staff were unaware of the shock episode.

article_limitations: No figures or supplements are listed in the source, so there are no pixels to review.

The method used to establish the C3, C6 and C7 dislocation is not stated.
